summary: Describes general considerations for deploying a stateful Path Computation Element, which tracks path state to do traffic-engineering calculations. It covers benefits, challenges and limitations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A stateful Path Computation Element (PCE) keeps information about active network paths as well as network topology. This can improve path planning, but the stored state must be synchronized with the network.

questions: what is an lsp state database
subtitle: Use cases and deployment trade-offs for a Path Computation Element that tracks active paths.

tldr.problem: A stateless PCE does not keep the full set of active paths, so independent requests may produce wasteful or unpredictable results.
tldr.mechanism: A stateful PCE keeps a database of active LSP state alongside its traffic-engineering database and may receive delegated control of paths.
tldr.outcome: The RFC surveys use cases and deployment challenges; it does not define the PCEP extensions itself.

facts.label: PCE delegation
facts.value: An LSP is delegated to one PCE at a time

today: RFC 8051 is Informational and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes applicability and use cases; the PCEP extensions for stateful PCE usage are covered in separate documents.

sections.title: Why a PCE Keeps Path State
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes traffic-engineered paths using network topology and resource information in a Traffic Engineering Database (TED). A stateful PCE also stores attributes of active Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in an LSP State Database.

The extra information lets a PCE consider how paths use resources and depend on one another. It also creates a need for reliable synchronization among the PCE, network, Path Computation Clients, and cooperating PCEs.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateful PCE plans with both a network map and a record of active paths. Keeping that record accurate requires coordination with the network.

sections.title: Passive, Active, and Delegated Control
sections.content:
A passive stateful PCE uses path information learned from clients to improve computations but does not actively update path state. An active stateful PCE may issue recommendations and change parameters for paths delegated to it.

Delegation gives a PCE temporary rights to modify some parameters of an LSP. The client that owns the LSP can delegate it, and one LSP is owned by one client at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: A passive PCE keeps information and gives better advice. An active PCE can also change a path when its owner delegates that control.

sections.title: Improving Path Placement
sections.content:
When separate clients request paths independently, request timing can produce poor use of network capacity. The RFC gives examples where global visibility and control of the order of changes can improve throughput, reduce unnecessary disruption, and make path selection more predictable.

A stateful PCE can also consider effects across paths during bandwidth changes, recovery, protection, and reoptimization. The RFC presents these as use cases, not as guarantees that every computation will be optimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Seeing all active paths helps a PCE consider how one route affects others. It can coordinate changes that separate clients would otherwise request independently.

sections.title: Other Uses for Stored State
sections.content:
The RFC discusses stateful PCEs for automatic bandwidth adjustment, scheduled bandwidth, recovery, virtual network topology maintenance, LSP reoptimization, resource defragmentation, point-to-multipoint paths, and impairment-aware optical routing.

For example, a PCE with path state can consider which backup resources are already shared or recompute several affected paths together. In some cases, it can use an LSP identifier instead of requiring a client to resend all path details.
sections.plainLanguage: Stored path information can support recovery, reoptimization, scheduling, and resource cleanup. The useful details depend on the network and the application.

sections.title: Deployment and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stateful and stateless PCEs can coexist, and deployments may use multiple stateful PCEs. An LSP is delegated to one PCE at a time. After a restart, the PCE needs to recover and resynchronize its LSP state.

The PCE's view may lag behind the network because state arrives from clients. Stateful PCE capabilities also expose more path information and control, so the documents defining the PCEP extensions need to consider authentication, encryption, and the extra attack surface.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateful PCE must recover its path records after a restart and keep them aligned with the network. Because it sees and may control more paths, its access needs protection.
